3. The importance of a gene for a given drug is calculated as the sum of
the weights for that gene over all Pareto-optimal formulae F divided
by the number of formulae in F.
Binarization threshold
A cell line is deﬁned as sensitive (resistant) based on its AUC value
being lower (larger) than a drug-speciﬁc threshold value b. This binar-
ization threshold is calculated (separately for each drug) in four steps
(K16). The description belowsummarizes the mainapproach adopted in
this work and it highlights any signiﬁcant differences to K16:
Step 1 (Up-sampling): For each of a set of N cell lines, 1,000 AUC
values are generated on the basis of the measured AUC value of the cell
line and its error assuming a normal distribution in log(AUC). K16 use
AUC instead of log(AUC).
Step 2 (Density Estimate): Subsequently, a 1-dimensional proba-
bility density function (pdf) of log(AUC) is calculated from the set of
1,000  N log(AUC) values via a Gaussian kernel density estimate with
a bandwidth of 0.5.
Step 3 (Modeling of resistant cell lines): The log(AUC) values of the
resistant cell lines are modeled as a normal distribution g with its mean
m given by the maximum of the pdf. The median distance from m of all
(upsampled) data points in the interval [q, m] is adopted as the
standard deviation s of g. Here, q is an auxiliary parameter used as
a proxy for b and calculated as described in K16.
Step 4 (Estimating b): The binarization threshold is set to the 10th
percentile of the distribution g. We chose the larger percentile com-
pared with the 5th percentile adopted by K16 to boost the fraction of
sensitive cell lines given the smaller number of cell lines (30–71 per
drug) of our sample.
LOBICO
Following the training stage, LOBICO provides, for each drug d, a
logical formula fd in disjunctive normal form with its propositional
variables given by the binary gene mutations (on/off interpreted as
True/False). The formula fd can be used to predict whether a new cell
line is likely sensitive or resistant to drug d. The on/off state of binary
gene mutations of the given cell line are inserted into the propositional
variables of fd and subsequently the formula is evaluated resulting in a
True or False statement. If fd evaluates to True (False), then the new cell
line is predicted to be sensitive (resistant) to drug d. The speciﬁc
formula fd provided by LOBICO is optimal in minimizing the weighted
mis-match between the predicted sensitivity and the actual sensitivity
of the provided cell lines to drug d. The complexity of the formula fd is
determined by two hyper-parameters K, M. Here, K is the maximum
number of conjunctions in the disjunction, while M is the maximum
number of literals per conjunction.
Figure of merit - AUC
LOBICO allows the addition of constraints on the minimal sensi-
tivity and minimal speciﬁcity of the logical formulae. Following K16,
we vary the lower bounds on the sensitivity and speciﬁcity in steps of
0.05 to ﬁnd formulae with the best possible values of sensitivity,
speciﬁcity, or both (i.e., Pareto efﬁcient formulae) for any given drug
with the help of a nested cross-validation. The sensitivity and spec-
iﬁcity values of these formulae trace out a curve in sensitivity–
speciﬁcity space and the AUC is used as ﬁgure of merit. During the
nested cross-validation, an inner 4-fold cross-validation is employed to
select the K, M hyper-parameters that result in the highest average
(over the inner folds) AUC. Given the tuned hyper-parameters,
LOBICO is then trained during the outer 5-fold cross-validation to
provide a formula for each sensitivity and speciﬁcity bound (provided a
formula satisfying the constraints can be found). Pareto efﬁcient
formulae areidentiﬁed among these formulae by solvingthe maximum
vector problem. A formula f is Pareto efﬁcient if there is no other
formula f’ that is better than f in the following sense. A formula f is
better than a formula f’ if: (i) f has higher sensitivity than f’ and its
speciﬁcity is at least as high as the one of f’, (ii) f has higher speciﬁcity
than f’ andits sensitivity is at least ashigh asthe oneof f’, or (iii) f hasthe
same sensitivity and speciﬁcity as f’ but contains a smaller number of
literals than f’. Subsequently, the sensitivities and speciﬁcities of the set
of Pareto efﬁcient formulae is calculated for each fold (test set) of the
outer cross-validation. The curve traced by the sensitivity and spec-
iﬁcity values of the Pareto efﬁcient formulae is the Pareto frontier.
Finally, the ﬁgure of merit and its error are given by the mean and by
the standard deviation of the area under the Pareto frontier for the 5
folds of the outer cross-validation.
Code availability
The scripts used tocarry out the threshold and LOBICO analysiscan
be found at:
https://github.com/sch2007/pancancer-pharmacogenomic-analy
sis.git.
LOBICO (Knijnenburg and colleagues 2016) is available at https://
github.com/tknijnen/LOBICO.
In vivo treatment studies
In vivo studies were carried out in accordance with the NIH
guidelines and a California Paciﬁc Medical Center (CPMC)-approved
Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee protocol (#18.08.03).
Four toﬁve, 8- to10-week-old female NSG mice (Jackson Laboratories,
Sacramento, CA) bearing subcutaneous PDX tumors were random-
ized according to initial tumor volume. They were treated with either
vehicle or 25 mg/kg ganetespib. Drugs were diluted in 4% DMSO,
4% Tween-80, and 92% saline. Treatment began when PDX tumor
volumes reached approximately 100 mm3. PDX-bearing NSG mice
were treated intraperitoneally daily for 5 consecutive days for approx-
imately 4 weeks or until PDX tumor volumes reached 2,000 mm3.
Tumors were measured approximately once to twice weekly by an
operator blinded to the treatment groups. Mice were housed in a single
ventilated cage in groups of four, provided environmental enrichment
materials, and free access to water and food. At the completion of
in vivo experiments, all animals were humanely killed using CO2
overdose followed by thoracotomy as outline by the American Vet-
erinary Medical Association guidelines for the euthanasia of animals.
Tumor volume was calculated as (length  width2)/2. The response
was determined by comparing tumor volume change at time t to its
baseline: % tumor volume change ¼ DVolt ¼ 100%  ((Vt – Vinitial)/
Vinitial). For comparison of drug response of vemurafenib and cobi-
metinib across PDX, the volume of the treated group for the last
measurement day was compared with the volume of the vehicle
(control) group and tumor volume (% Control) was determined:
100%  [1 þ (Tumor volume treated – Tumor volume vehicle)/ Tumor
volume vehicle]. Four to 5 mice were used for studies based on sample
size calculations from preliminary studies.
Statistical analyses
For in vivo experiments, differences in tumor growth between
treatment groups were evaluated using Two-way ANOVA repeated
measures, and Tukey multiple comparisons test.
Data availability
The data generated in this study are available within the article and
its Supplementary Data ﬁles.

publications.results:
Establishment of PDXC models from tumors
78 patient-derived tumor cultures were established across nine
cancers: glioblastoma, colorectal, ovarian, pancreatic, melanoma,
cholangiocarcinoma, gall bladder, and breast (Fig. 1A). A majority
of the cultures were PDXC developed from PDX, but in some cases
enough tissue was collected to develop primary patient-derived
tumor cultures (PDC) for analysis. As previously demonstrated, for
speciﬁc drugs there is highly concordant drug sensitivity across
derivatives (3). For generation of PDX, human tumor tissue samples
were received within 1 to 2 hours after resection and tumor material
was implanted in NSG mice for expansion (Fig. 1B). After suc-
cessful expansion, PDX tissue was collected from mice and PDXC
were established (Fig. 1B). PDX and corresponding PDXC were
analyzed for somatic mutation using the Illumina TruSeq Amplicon
48 gene cancer panel (Fig. 1C), and PDXC were evaluated for
sensitivity to a panel of drugs using HTDS (Fig. 1D). The phar-
macologic and genomic data are combined to create logic models to
predict sensitivity of a given cell line to a drug based on DNA
mutation status (Fig. 1E).
The 78 tumors were obtained from 34 men and 44 women (Sup-
plementary Table S2), with ages ranging from 40 to 90s, and obtained
from various sites. Patients were treatment naive or had speciﬁc
treatment histories for each cancer. The tumor samples collected,
which were used to derive PDC, PDX, and PDXC, reﬂect patient
populations receiving current standard of care.
Concordance of somatic mutations across patients and PDXs
correlates with VAF
For four cancers, melanoma (Fig. 2A), glioblastoma (Fig. 2B),
colorectal (Fig. 2C), and pancreatic (Fig. 2D), there was enough tumor
tissue available from the original patient sample and corresponding
PDX models to perform NGS. A total of 23 matched samples were
analyzed. The nomenclature used for xenograft passaged tumors was X
(ﬁrst generation) and X1 (second generation), corresponding to serial
passaging in vivo. A sequencing library targeting 212 amplicons in
48 genes was generated using the Illumina TruSeq Amplicon – Cancer
Panel. In agreement with previously published Cancer Genome
analyses (18–21) lineage speciﬁc mutations were identiﬁed for indi-
vidual cancers. For example, tumor tissues from the patients and their
corresponding PDXs in melanoma contained BRAF, NRAS, PTEN,
KIT, and TP53 mutations, GBM samples contained PTEN and EGFR
mutations, colorectal cancer samples contained APC and EGFR muta-
tions, and all pancreatic cancer samples contained KRAS mutations.
Among the ﬁve ovarian cancer specimens tested in this study, three
were high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), one was later
categorized as squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix (OVCA0033)
and one was a yolk sac tumor (OVCA0027). The HGSOC commonly
carry TP53 mutations, however, these mutations were not detected in
our samples, which may be the result of using a cancer panel that does
not cover all exons (14).
We previously published in melanoma that an increase in VAF
corresponded to an increase in stability of speciﬁc mutations across the
patient tumor, corresponding PDX, and subsequent generations of

PDXs (14). We, therefore, examined this phenomenon across addi-
tional cancers including additional melanoma samples. For melano-
ma, in patient tumor and ﬁrst generation PDX the total concordance
was 58% for VAF ≥10% and 91% for VAF ≥25%. For glioblastoma, in
patient tumor and ﬁrst generation PDX the total concordance was 65%
for VAF ≥10% and 100% for VAF ≥25%. For colorectal cancer, in
patient tumor and ﬁrst generation PDX the total concordance was 85%
for VAF ≥10% and 100% for VAF ≥25%. For pancreatic cancer, in
patient tumor and ﬁrst generation PDX the total concordance was
100% for VAF ≥10% and 100% for VAF ≥25%. Our data demonstrate
that PDXs harbor somatic mutations in cancer-driving genes as
expected in accordance with TCGA data. Furthermore, the concor-
dance of somatic mutations across patient tumor and matched PDXs
increases as VAF increases. The ﬁdelity of cancer-driving gene muta-
tions across human and PDX samples suggests that responses to
antitumor agents across derivatives would be conserved.
Evaluation of PDXC response to antitumor agents using HTDS
19 antitumor agents were evaluated across 78 patient-derived tumor
cultures, constituting 9 different cancers (Fig. 3A). Tumors were
cultured as tumorspheres in 384-well plates, treated with drugs for
3 days and assessed for cell viability. Because a precision medicine
platform was being developed, we chose our maximum concentration
in the assay to correspond to the maximum plasma concentration
(Cmax) at the highest single dose recommended on the basis of clinical
trials when the information was available, and when the drug was not
limited by solubility (Supplementary Table S1). After drug treatment,
the area under the dose–response curve (AUC) with corresponding
CIs was calculated. As cell viability/proliferation is decreased, the AUC
is reduced (22, 23).
Past studies, and recent large scale screening efforts, demonstrate
that AUC is more effective than either calculating the potency and
efﬁcacy of a drug across multiple cancer lines, because AUC takes into

Notable individual PDXC responses to speciﬁc drugs, as well as
lineage-speciﬁc drug responses where observed. For example, in
BRAF-mutant melanoma there was a strong response to both BRAF
and MEK inhibitors, and as expected, melanomas harboring wild-type
BRAF were insensitive to BRAF inhibitors. The BRAF and MEK
inhibitor responses in PDXC and corresponding PDX have been
previously described by our group in a smaller cohort of melanoma
samples (14). Pan-cancer HTDS analysis also demonstrated notable
higher drug sensitivities to dinaciclib (CDK inhibitor), vorinostat
(histone deacetylase inhibitor), sapanesertib (PI3K/mTOR inhibitor),
gedatolisip (PI3K/mTOR inhibitor) and ganetespib (heat shock pro-
tein 90 inhibitor; Fig. 3A). Ganetespib has been assessed in multiple
clinical trials against various cancers, demonstrating the ability to
produce partial response and stable disease in a subset of patients in
each trial (24). Because HSP90 protects cells under conditions of stress,
HSP90 inhibitors have the ability to sensitize cells to the toxic effects of
chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Therefore, multiple drug com-
bination clinical trials are underway with promising initial ﬁnd-
ings (24). To determine whether the inhibitory activity of ganetespib
in culture (Fig. 3B) would be recapitulated in vivo (Fig. 3C), we treated
mice bearing PDX OVCA0032X with ganetespib. OVCA0032 is an
epithelial carcinoma with a wild-type p53. In PDXC OVCA0032X,
ganetespib produced a potent and efﬁcacious inhibition of cell via-
bility/proliferation. In agreement with the activity observed in PDXC,
we found that ganetespib produced a sustained inhibition of tumor
growth in mice bearing PDX OVCA0032X (Fig. 3C).
In GBM, colorectal, ovarian, pancreatic, melanoma, and lung
PDXCs lineage-speciﬁc sensitivity to drugs were evaluated using
Wilcoxon analysis (Fig. 3D). Again, sensitivity for BRAF and MEK
inhibitors was identiﬁed for BRAF-mutant melanoma, and sensitivity
to MEK inhibitors was also identiﬁed for wild-type BRAF melanoma.
Additional lineage speciﬁc drug responses identiﬁed included, cobi-
metinib sensitivity in lung cancer, and vorinostat sensitivity in mel-
anoma, buparlisib and dinaciclib sensitivity in ovarian cancer, and
everolimus sensitivity in pancreatic cancer. It should also be noted that
breast cancer PDXC BRC0013, containing a EGFR R108K mutation,
had a unique sensitivity to the HER2 inhibitor lapatinib, as expected.
It has been reported in serum-derived cell lines that for speciﬁc
drugs the growth rate (GR) of cells may confound the comparison of
standard pharmacology measures (IC50, Emax, AUC) between cell
lines (17). Modiﬁed pharmacologic analysis (e.g., GR50 and GRmax) to
account for proliferation rate were proposed and were expected to
more correctly facilitate the discovery of biomarkers that predict drug

at least one cell division over a period of 3 days, 25% (n ¼ 40) of PDXC
show limited cell division as assessed by calculating the growth index
(Supplementary Fig. S1). These growth characteristics are more rep-
resentative of patient tumors that are often slow growing. GR analysis
was therefore not appropriate for many PDXC, because the underlying
equations are dependent on a signiﬁcant increase in the cell population
in the control groups over time (17). We therefore calculated the AUC
and standard pharmacologic measures to compare drug sensitivity
across all primary patient-derived tumor models tested.
Binarization threshold determination to classify drug sensitivity
and resistance for logic modeling
We used LOBICO, a computational approach that infers small and
easily interpretable logic models of binary input features that explain a
continuous output variable (15). In the context of this investigation,
this model was used to uncover logic combinations of multiple DNA
mutations that would be more predictive of drug response than single
DNA mutation predictors. Single predictors (e.g., a DNA mutation)
are generally less accurate predicting drug response because of the
complexity of biological pathways driving cancer.
Our analysis was based on screening 19 drugs across 78 patient-
derived tumor cultures from 9 different cancers, and each of the
tumors underwent a targeted resequencing assay for detection of
somatic mutations in cancer genome hotspots. The AUC with corre-
sponding conﬁdence limits was obtained after 3 days treatment with a
drug and served as the continuous output variable. LOBICO was
applied to the AUCs and corresponding conﬁdence limits of each drug
separately. For the ﬁrst step of LOBICO, a binarization threshold for
the output variable is calculated (Fig. 4A; Supplementary Fig. S2,
Supplementary Table S3). This threshold is used to separate the PDXC
into two groups: PDXC sensitive and PDXC resistant to drug (Fig. 4B;
Supplementary Table S4). LOBICO ﬁnds an optimal logic function of
binary mutation features that minimizes the error, which is deﬁned as

this method has been used to deﬁne resistant and sensitive populations
of cell lines, it has never been validated in vivo to determine the extent
to which the classiﬁcation predicts response of a tumor in a preclinical
mouse xenograft model. Validating the drug resistant and sensitive
classiﬁcation obtained using PDXC (culture), in PDX (in vivo) models,
provides increased conﬁdence in the relevance of the binarization
threshold ﬁndings obtained in culture (PDXC).
We chose PDXC and corresponding PDX derived from 8 BRAF-
mutant melanoma for our analysis. We evaluated the resistant
and sensitive classiﬁcation of vemurafenib and cobimetinib in PDXC
to the response observed in vivo (Fig. 4C and D). The AUC-derived
binarization threshold predicted for vemurafenib and cobimetinib in
the PDXC was 2.33 and 2.14, respectively. The log AUC values were:
vemurafenib (MM358X1 ¼ 2.34, MM337X2 ¼ 2.42, MM321X1 ¼
2.22, MM302X ¼ 2.39, MM313X ¼ 2.11, MM314X1 ¼ 2.0, MM334X ¼
1.34, MM325X ¼ 1.29) and cobimetinib (MM358X1 ¼ 2.32,
MM337X1 ¼ 2.15, MM321X1 ¼ 2.22, MM302X ¼ 1.79, MM313X ¼
2.13, MM314X1 ¼ 1.71, MM334X ¼ 1.39, MM325X ¼ 1.12). The log
AUC values for MM358X1, MM337X2, MM321X1, and MM302 were
derived previously (14).
We then compared the response of the corresponding PDX models
to vemurafenib and cobimetinib using previously published data from
our group (14). The drug responses in vivo were originally evaluated by
measuring tumor volume (mm3). In the current study, the tumor
volume (mm3) of the treated group for the last measurement day was
compared with the tumor volume of the vehicle (control) group and
tumor volume (% Control) was calculated. These data were used to
cross compare the response of all 8 PDX to vemurafenib and cobi-
metinib (Fig. 4C and D). Cobimetinib produced robust inhibition of
tumor growth in the models falling under the sensitive classiﬁcation
(Fig. 4D). Inhibition of tumor progression was also observed in a
subset of models falling under the insensitive classiﬁcation, but to a
lesser extent than observed in the sensitive classiﬁcation. For vemur-
afenib, the classiﬁcations deﬁned tumors sensitive and resistant
to treatment in vivo (Fig. 4C). Overall, the binarization threshold
sensitive classiﬁcation determined in culture (PDXC) identiﬁes tumors
that respond to drug in vivo (PDX).
Logic models of DNA mutations to predict drug sensitivity
Once binarization threshold sensitive classiﬁcation were deter-
mined, we next used LOBICO to address the question of how well
drug sensitivity can be explained by logic models of genes evaluated in
the cancer gene panel-based NGS.The mutational data for each sample
is inputted as a binary feature, where 0 is the absence of a DNA
mutation (e.g., wild-type BRAF) and 1 is the presence of a DNA
mutation (e.g., BRAF V6000E) (Supplementary Table S5). During
training, which is carried out separately for each drug, LOBICO
requires both the mutational data and the AUC data for the cell lines.
The AUC data are provided as raw data calculated using a standard
formula (Materials and Methods) or as scaled data from 0 to 1
(Supplementary Table S5). Our analysis incorporated the raw AUC
data. Following the training stage, LOBICO provides, for each drug d,
logical formulae in disjunctive normal form with its propositional
variables given by the binary gene mutations (on/off interpreted as
True/False). These formulae predict whether a new cell line is likely
sensitive or resistant to the considered drug depending on whether
they evaluate to True or False. The logic models provided by LOBICO
are optimal in minimizing the weighted mis-match between the
predicted sensitivity and the actual sensitivity of the provided cell
lines to drug d.
LOBICO allows to put constraints on the sensitivity and speciﬁcity
of logic models. Following (15), we vary the lower bounds on the
sensitivity and speciﬁcity in steps of 0.05 to ﬁnd logic models with the
best possible values of sensitivity, speciﬁcity, or both for any given
drug. The sensitivity and speciﬁcity values of these models trace out a
curve in sensitivity–speciﬁcity space, the Pareto frontier, and the AUC
is then interpreted as ﬁgure of merit (Fig. 5A and B; Supplementary
Fig. S3). To minimize overﬁtting and arrive at a more robust estimate
of the ﬁgure of merit we employ nested cross-validation, consisting of
an inner 4-fold cross-validation to tune the hyper-parameters of the
logic models and an outer 5-fold cross-validation to robustly estimate
the ﬁgure of merit and its error (Supplementary Table S6).
Figure 5B shows the Pareto frontier for the drug dabrafenib. The
Pareto frontier for the additional drugs is presented in Supplementary
Fig. S3. The area under the speciﬁcity – sensitivity curve for dabrafenib
is 0.92 (0.03) if applied to the cell lines in the training and validation
set, and 0.87 (0.14) if applied to the cell lines in the test set during
cross-validation. This indicates that logical models are able to predict
whether cell lines are resistant or not to those drugs with reasonable
accuracy. One of the high scoring logic models for dabrafenib is the
single gene BRAF as is expected for this selective inhibitor, validating
the prediction potential of the model. The predictions for all drugs are
presented in Supplementary Table S6.
The curve in sensitivity–speciﬁcity space (Pareto frontier) shown
in Fig. 5B is associated with a list F of formulae with high sensitivity,
speciﬁcity or both. By analyzing these formulae for each drug, we can
identify genes that help in identifying sensitive and resistant cell lines.
The importance of a gene for a given drug is calculated as follows. First,
the weight of a gene is calculated for each formula f from F. Each gene is
assigned a weight, where each mutated gene (e.g., BRAF V600E) counts
as 1. A gene such as BRAF could have various mutations based on the
NGS panel, which covers multiple mutation hotspots (e.g., BRAF
V600E, BRAF V600K, etc.). Each gene that is not mutated (e.g.,
BRAF or wild-type BRAF) counts 1. If a gene occurs multiple
times in a formula the individual weights are added (an alternative
option would be to average the weights). For instance, in the formula
BRAF & KRAS | BRAF & KIT, BRAF has weight 1 and BRAF has a
weight of 1, therefore the sum of BRAF ¼ (1 þ 1) ¼ 0), KRAS has
weight 1, and KIT has weight 1. Next, the importance of a gene for a
given drug is calculated as the sum of the weights for that gene for each
formula in F divided by the number of formulae in F. Fig. 5C and
Supplementary Table S7 show the gene(s) of importance for each drug.
As shown above, cell lines with BRAF gene mutations are predicted
to be sensitive to treatment with MEK and BRAF inhibitors. As expect
BRAF and MEK inhibitors ranked with high scores for the BRAF gene,
logic models contained BRAF alone or in combination with additional
genes and resistance was predicted by RAS mutations (ref. 25; See also
Supplementary Table S7). EGFR was scored for erlotinib but not
afatanib, the lack of association was the result of tumors not containing
EGFR mutations shown to infer sensitization to the drug such as
Del19/L858R (26). Of note, a gene of importance for the HSP90
inhibitor ganetespib was FGFR3, and many logic models included the
presence of FGFR3 mutations (Supplementary Table S7). Upon review
of the individual DNA mutations, we found multiple cancers (pan-
creatic, lung, and melanoma) deﬁned as sensitive to ganetespib that
contained FGFR3 30_prime UTR variants (Supplementary Table S8).
FGFR3 has been shown to be a strong HSP90 client compared with
other FGFR receptors, and depends on HSP90 for stability and
function (27). In addition, vorinostat ranked with a high score for
BRAF, and had multiple logic models that included BRAF mutations
(Supplementary Table S7), thereby demonstrating a lineage-speciﬁc

publications.conclusions:
The evaluation of pharmacologic sensitivities of cancer cells
paired with their genomic proﬁle provides a powerful platform for
precision medicine oncology. Over the last decade, multiple inves-
tigations have demonstrated the utility of pharmacogenomics stud-
ies in determining gene(s) predicting sensitivity and resistance to
single and drug combination therapies (4, 8, 32–35). Many of the
large-scale studies have used data from serum-derived cancer cell
lines, including the notable investigations using data derived from
CCLE and GDSC studies (8, 32–36). More recent investigations
have also used similar approaches using patient-derived primary
tumor cultures (3). As opposed to serum-derived cell lines, primary
patient-derived tumor cultures have been shown to more faithfully
recapitulate the genotype and phenotype of the original patient’s
tumor (9–13, 37–39). In addition, a recent study showed that a pan-
cancer analysis, using over 400 unique PDCs, not propagated in
mice, could be used to predict clinical response (3).
Many different statistical and bioinformatics approaches have been
examined to enhance pharmacogenomics prediction (3, 40–42). For
instance, machine learning based modeling approaches such as logical
models, elastic net regression, and random forests as well as ANOVA
models have been successfully applied to predict drug response based
on genetic information (3, 15, 32). LOBICO has been used to explore
pharmacogenomicrelationshipsusingserum-derivedcelllines(15,32),
but this study represents the ﬁrst to use LOBICO for analysis of
primary patient-derived tumors.
In this investigation, we performed a pharmacogenomic analysis of
patient-derived tumor cultures, including PDXC. In contrast to PDC,
they are easily expandable for future mechanistic studies both in
culture and in vivo. In addition, in comparison with studying multiple
drug–gene interactions in PDX models, PDXC offer a lower cost
resource for this type of analysis and are amenable to HTDS analysis
of single and drug combination therapies. We established 78 patient-
derived tumor cultures across 9 cancers. Our data demonstrate that the
tumors harbor somatic mutations in cancer-driving genes, and the

concordance of somatic mutations across patient tumor and matched
PDXs increases as VAF increases. Nineteen antitumor agents were
evaluated across 78 patient-derived tumor cultures, constituting 9
different cancers using clinically relevant drug exposures (42). Because
the patient-derived tumor cultures do not contain components of the
microenvironment, we focused our analysis primarily on agents
known to produce antitumor activity by directly targeting tumor cells.
Response to PDXC were recapitulated in PDX models. Lineage-
speciﬁc drug responses were identiﬁed, for instance, response of
melanoma to BRAF and MEK inhibitors. Additional lineage speciﬁc
drug responses identiﬁed included, vorinostat (HDACi) sensitivity in
melanoma, cobimetinib (MEKi) sensitivity in lung cancer, buparlisib
(PI3K) and dinaciclib (CDK1/2/5/9) sensitivity in ovarian cancer, and
everolimus (mTOR) sensitivity in pancreatic cancer.
We next usedlogic modeling anda gene score calculation touncover
gene alterations, both single and combination, that predict response to
speciﬁc drugs. As a ﬁrst step, binarization thresholds were determined
to classify drug sensitivity and resistance in culture for logic modeling.
While this sensitivity classiﬁcation in culture, and additional drug
sensitivity classiﬁcations based on z-score calculations (3), would
theoretically deﬁne responses in vivo, they have never been tested in
detail in preclinical mouse models of cancer. A unique aspect of this
study was to evaluate the correlation between the sensitivity classiﬁ-
cation of BRAF and MEK inhibitors in culture in comparison with
response in vivo. Overall, the binarization threshold sensitive classi-
ﬁcation determined in PDXC predicted a drug response in the
corresponding PDX model. However, for the MEK inhibitor cobime-
tinib, some tumors falling under the resistant classiﬁcation did respond
to drug in vivo. This classiﬁcation may be further improved by
including more cell lines.
Once binarization threshold sensitive classiﬁcations were deter-
mined, logic models of DNA mutations were developed to predict drug
sensitivity and speciﬁcity. The ﬁgure of merit is the AUC of the ROC
curve in the sensitivity–speciﬁcity plane (15). This ROC curve is the
Pareto frontier of LOBICO-optimal solutions subject to minimal
sensitivity and speciﬁcity constraints. Genes of importance for each
drug were then determined by calculating the average signed occur-
rence of that gene (þ1 for mutated type, 1 for wild-type) in the
LOBICO-optimal formulae.
As expected, BRAF and MEK inhibitors ranked with high scores
for the BRAF gene, logic models contained BRAF alone or in
combination with additional genes and resistance was predicted by
RAS mutations (25). There were multiple novel gene–drug associa-
tions, and logic models of interest uncovered by the analysis. For
example, a gene of importance for tumor cell sensitivity to ganetespib
was FGFR3, and many logic models included the presence of FGFR3
mutations. In FGFR3-driven bladder cancer, ganetespib produces
potent cytotoxicity comparable with the pan-FGFR tyrosine kinase
inhibitor BGJ398 (43). How the 3_prime UTR variants observed in
our PDXC deﬁned as sensitive to ganetespib affect the HSP90/
receptor interaction remains to be determined, but provides an
example of how pharmacogenomic analysis using the described
platform may identify biomarkers of response to speciﬁc drugs. In
addition, a gene of importance for sensitivity to vorinostat was
BRAF. Multiple logic models for this drug included BRAF mutations,
and there was also a lineage speciﬁc drug sensitivity in BRAF-wild-
type melanoma. This inhibitory activity of vorinostat alone and in
combination with other antitumor agents has been shown in a HTDS
of melanoma PDC (5); however, there were no genomic correlates
described for this activity. As discussed, sensitivity to vorinostat
has been reported in melanoma through modulation of ROS, or
production of excessive DNA damage (28, 29). Of interest, BRAF
mutation (common in melanoma) was labeled a high predictor of
sensitivity to vorinostat, whereas TP53 mutation denoted resistance
to the drug. The CHK inhibitor LY2603618 also ranked with a high
score for BRAF and this drug has been shown to be effective at
inhibiting tumor growth in vemurafenib-resistant melanoma (30).
Resistance to PI3K and mTOR inhibitors was also predicted by APC
mutations in agreement with past pharmacogenomics analysis of
PDC (3). The CDK inhibitor dinaciclib can control the expression
of multiple short-lived proteins involved in cancer cell survival (31).
It had unique logic models where sensitivity was predicted by
the absence of mutations in multiple cancer driving genes including
ATM, TP53, BRAF, SMAD4, or was predicted by the presence
of EGFR, MET, NRAS, FGFR3 mutations. This may relate to the
more global transcriptional inhibition produced by dinaciclib.
Intriguingly, our data indicate that many of our ovarian PDXC
fall within these classiﬁcations leading to lineage-speciﬁc sensitivity
to dinaciclib.
The limited number of drug-sensitive PDXCs poses a challenge for
the present analysis. However, even with this issue, we were able to
observe strong drug–gene association with classical genes such as
BRAF. In addition, multiple novel gene–drug associations and logic
models of interest were uncovered by the analysis. One challenge is that
the calculation of the AUC requires at least one sensitive and one
resistant cell line per training/validation/testing data set to calculate
sensitivities and speciﬁcities. As a form of mitigation, we distributed
sensitive and resistant cell lines in approximately equal proportions
among the training/validation/testing data sets during cross valida-
tion. As more PDXC drug–gene data is added to the model, error in
AUC estimates will be reduced. Furthermore, increasing the number of
cell lines analyzed will also enable the use of more ﬂexible LOBICO
formulae (i.e., larger values for K and M) thus potentially increasing the
AUC ﬁgure of merit. Even with these caveats, multiple lineage and gene
(s) speciﬁc drug sensitivities were identiﬁed as described above,
including novel associations.
Overall, we performed a pharmacologic analysis of antitumor
agents used at clinically relevant doses in expandable primary
patient-derived tumors across cancers. Using logic modeling, the
pharmacologic data were combined with DNA mutational analysis
of cancer driving genes in the primary patient-derived tumors to
determine somatic gene mutation(s) deﬁning response to antitumor
agents. Taken together, these results describe a novel strategy for
developing a pharmacogenomic platform for precision medicine
oncology using expandable primary patient-derived tumors.

publications.title: Therapeutic targeting of prenatal pontine ID1 signaling in diffuse midline glioma
publications.abstract:
Background.  Diffuse midline gliomas (DMG) are highly invasive brain tumors with rare survival beyond two years 
past diagnosis and limited understanding of the mechanism behind tumor invasion. Previous reports demonstrate 
upregulation of the protein ID1 with H3K27M and ACVR1 mutations in DMG, but this has not been confirmed in 
human tumors or therapeutically targeted.
Methods. Whole exome, RNA, and ChIP-sequencing was performed on the ID1 locus in DMG tissue. Scratch-
assay migration and transwell invasion assays of cultured cells were performed following shRNA-mediated ID1-
knockdown. In vitro and in vivo genetic and pharmacologic [cannabidiol (CBD)] inhibition of ID1 on DMG tumor 
growth was assessed. Patient-reported CBD dosing information was collected.

PPK-IUE Model of pHGG (Pediatric High-grade 
Gliomas)
All animal studies were conducted according to guidelines 
approved by the University Committee on Use and Care of 
Animals (UCUCA) at the University of Michigan. In-utero elec-
troporation (IUE) was performed using sterile technique on 
isoflurane/oxygen anesthetized pregnant CD1 females at em-
bryonic stage E13.5, using established methodology.13,14 In this 
study, we injected the following four plasmids together: [1] 
PBase, [2] PB-CAG-DNp53-Ires-Luciferase (dominant negative 
TP53 or TP53 hereafter), [3] PB-CAG-PdgfraD842V (PDGFRA 
D842V), and [4] PB-CAG-H3.3 K27M- (H3K27M), referred to as 
the “PPK”-IUE pHGG model15 (Supplementary Material).
Whole Exome and Transcriptome Sequencing 
(Sick Kids, Toronto)
Use of patient tissues was approved by the Hospital for Sick 
Children (Toronto) Research Ethics Board. WES/WGS (accession 
EGAS00001000575) from 34 DMG samples plus 18 matched 
normal brains were used. The total RNA Library Prep with Ribo-
Zero Gold Kit (Illumina, CA, USA) was used and paired end 
sequencing generated with Illumina HiSeq 2500 machines (acces-
sion EGAD00001006450)16 (Supplementary Material).
MiNT-ChIP-sequencing of Tumor Tissue
Analyses for the two classical histone modifications 
H3K27ac and H3K27me3, representing accessible and 
repressed chromatin states, respectively, were per-
formed as part of a MiNT-ChIP analysis for 9 tumor sam-
ples of DMG patients in comparison to a control tissue 
sample of healthy pons according to the protocol pub-
lished by Buenstro et al. (Supplementary Material).
Single-cell RNA Sequencing (scRNA-
seq) Analysis from Developing Brain and 
H3K27M-mutant DMGs
Single-cell gene expression data and their clusters in the 
developing brain were obtained from GSE133531 (mouse 
pons), GSE120046 (human pons, gestational week 8–28), 
and GSE144462 (human cortex, gestational week 21–26) 
(Supplementary Material).
Native ChIP-qPCR
Native ChIP-qPCR was performed on post-mortem tissue 
using antibodies against H3K27ac (2  μl, Cat#07360, 
Millipore Sigma), H3K27me3 (1  μg, Cat#07449, Millipore 
Sigma), and control IgG (2 μg Cat#12370, Millipore Sigma) 
(Supplementary Material).
Invasion Assay
Invasion assays were performed using growth factor-reduced 
Matrigel invasion chambers with 8  μm pores (Cat#354483, 
Corning) as described in previously published work.17
Migration (Scratch) Assay
Migration assays were performed following a previously 
published protocol with slight modifications.18 Cells were 
seeded in 6-well plates and grown to approximately 80% 
confluence. Scratches were made using a 200 μl pipette tip 
and migration was then monitored using the IncuCyte® 
live-cell analysis system.
CBD Treatment Studies In In Vivo PPK-IUE and 
DIPGXIIIP* Mouse Model
Mice harboring IUE-generated PPK HGG tumors were treated 
with cannabidiol (CBD) when tumors reached logarithmic 
growth phase (minimum 2 × 106 photons/s via bioluminescent 
imaging). Mice litters from each experimental group were 
randomized to treatment with: (A) 15 mg/kg CBD (10% CBD 
suspended in Ethanol, 80% DPBS, 10% Tween-80) and (B) con-
trol treatment (10% Ethanol, 80% DPBS, 10% Tween-80). Mice 
were treated via intraperitoneal injection 5  days/week until 
morbidity all control mice (Supplementary Material).

tional program that is therapeutically targetable with CBD.
Key Points
•	 ID1 is found to be a novel therapeutic target in DMG.
•	 ID1 is found to be epigenetically upregulated in H3K27M-DMG.
•	 Preliminary data suggest that therapeutic targeting of ID1 decreases tumor cell 
invasion/migration and tumor growth in human and murine pHGG models.
Diffuse midline gliomas (DMG) are lethal pediatric brain 
tumors that originate in the midline brain structures, and 
have a median survival of 10–11  months.1 Standard of 
care consists of palliative radiation, and experimental 
chemotherapies have yet to demonstrate additional bene-
fits. Even with the advent of precision-based medicine, clin-
ical trials targeting specific molecular targets are lacking, 
highlighting the need to identify novel therapeutic targets.
As many as 80% of DMGs harbor a lysine-to-methionine 
substitution (H3K27M) in Histone H3.3 (H3.3A) or Histone 
H3.1 (H3C2).1,2 H3K27M now defines a distinct sub-
group in DMG and is associated with worse prognoses.3 
The H3K27M mutation represses the polycomb repres-
sive complex 2 (PRC2), resulting in global reduction of 
H3K27me3 (with focal gains),4 and global increases in acet-
ylation of H3K27 (H3K27ac) with focal losses, associated 
with upregulation of tumor-driving genes.5
Constitutive expression of Inhibitor of DNA binding (ID) 
proteins has been shown to inhibit the differentiation of 
multiple tissues.6 ID proteins dimerize with basic helix-loop-
helix (bHLH) transcription factors, preventing DNA binding.7 
bHLH transcription factors are key regulators of tissue and 
lineage-specific gene expression.8 Overexpression of the 
Inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1) gene has been tied to the 
pathogenesis and invasiveness of multiple human can-
cers.8,9 ID1 is associated with downstream activin A  re-
ceptor type 1 (ACVR1) signaling, which itself is mutated/
activated in 25% of DMGs,10–12 indicating a potential role for 
ID1. Prior studies have shown H3K27M and ACVR-mutation 
upregulate ID1 in cultured human astrocytes and murine 
models of DMG.10,11 Invasion into normal brain tissue is a 
pathognomonic feature of DMG, but its regulation remains 
poorly understood. Further, analysis of ID1 in human DMG 
preclinical models, and its regulation and targetability, have 
not been previously investigated.
In the present study, we show that DMGs demonstrate 
epigenetic activation and increased expression of ID1, in-
fluenced most strongly by H3K27M mutational status and 
brain location. ID1-high DMG tumor cells most closely re-
semble developing human and murine prenatal pontine 
astrocyte precursors with an activated “migratory” tran-
scriptional program. Genetic and pharmacologic (CBD) 
suppression of ID1 decreases invasion, and to a greater ex-
tent, migration, and improves survival in multiple preclin-
ical DMG models. These findings represent an exciting new 
direction for understanding the regulation and targetability 
of invasion in DMG, with broad implications for thera-
peutic targeting of solid tumors with ID1 upregulation.
Importance of the Study
Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are incurable pediatric 
brain tumors, and there is a need to identify novel ge-
netic targets that can be exploited therapeutically. We 
show that ID1 drives DMG cell invasion and migration. 
ID1-knockdown (genetic and pharmacologic) in human 
DMG cells reduces tumor growth and improves survival 
of mice. Taken together, our data demonstrate that CBD, 
which inhibits ID1, affects multiple malignant pheno-
types of DMG, including proliferation, invasion, and mi-
gration. The effects of CBD on DMG are mediated by 
both ID1-dependent and ID1-independent mechanisms. 
These results lay the groundwork for additional investi-
gations targeting ID1 and hold potentially major impli-
cations for future clinical trials.

Materials and Methods
PPK-IUE Model of pHGG (Pediatric High-grade 
Gliomas)
All animal studies were conducted according to guidelines 
approved by the University Committee on Use and Care of 
Animals (UCUCA) at the University of Michigan. In-utero elec-
troporation (IUE) was performed using sterile technique on 
isoflurane/oxygen anesthetized pregnant CD1 females at em-
bryonic stage E13.5, using established methodology.13,14 In this 
study, we injected the following four plasmids together: [1] 
PBase, [2] PB-CAG-DNp53-Ires-Luciferase (dominant negative 
TP53 or TP53 hereafter), [3] PB-CAG-PdgfraD842V (PDGFRA 
D842V), and [4] PB-CAG-H3.3 K27M- (H3K27M), referred to as 
the “PPK”-IUE pHGG model15 (Supplementary Material).
Whole Exome and Transcriptome Sequencing 
(Sick Kids, Toronto)
Use of patient tissues was approved by the Hospital for Sick 
Children (Toronto) Research Ethics Board. WES/WGS (accession 
EGAS00001000575) from 34 DMG samples plus 18 matched 
normal brains were used. The total RNA Library Prep with Ribo-
Zero Gold Kit (Illumina, CA, USA) was used and paired end 
sequencing generated with Illumina HiSeq 2500 machines (acces-
sion EGAD00001006450)16 (Supplementary Material).
MiNT-ChIP-sequencing of Tumor Tissue
Analyses for the two classical histone modifications 
H3K27ac and H3K27me3, representing accessible and 
repressed chromatin states, respectively, were per-
formed as part of a MiNT-ChIP analysis for 9 tumor sam-
ples of DMG patients in comparison to a control tissue 
sample of healthy pons according to the protocol pub-
lished by Buenstro et al. (Supplementary Material).
Single-cell RNA Sequencing (scRNA-
seq) Analysis from Developing Brain and 
H3K27M-mutant DMGs
Single-cell gene expression data and their clusters in the 
developing brain were obtained from GSE133531 (mouse 
pons), GSE120046 (human pons, gestational week 8–28), 
and GSE144462 (human cortex, gestational week 21–26) 
(Supplementary Material).
Native ChIP-qPCR
Native ChIP-qPCR was performed on post-mortem tissue 
using antibodies against H3K27ac (2  μl, Cat#07360, 
Millipore Sigma), H3K27me3 (1  μg, Cat#07449, Millipore 
Sigma), and control IgG (2 μg Cat#12370, Millipore Sigma) 
(Supplementary Material).
Invasion Assay
Invasion assays were performed using growth factor-reduced 
Matrigel invasion chambers with 8  μm pores (Cat#354483, 
Corning) as described in previously published work.17
Migration (Scratch) Assay
Migration assays were performed following a previously 
published protocol with slight modifications.18 Cells were 
seeded in 6-well plates and grown to approximately 80% 
confluence. Scratches were made using a 200 μl pipette tip 
and migration was then monitored using the IncuCyte® 
live-cell analysis system.
CBD Treatment Studies In In Vivo PPK-IUE and 
DIPGXIIIP* Mouse Model
Mice harboring IUE-generated PPK HGG tumors were treated 
with cannabidiol (CBD) when tumors reached logarithmic 
growth phase (minimum 2 × 106 photons/s via bioluminescent 
imaging). Mice litters from each experimental group were 
randomized to treatment with: (A) 15 mg/kg CBD (10% CBD 
suspended in Ethanol, 80% DPBS, 10% Tween-80) and (B) con-
trol treatment (10% Ethanol, 80% DPBS, 10% Tween-80). Mice 
were treated via intraperitoneal injection 5  days/week until 
morbidity all control mice (Supplementary Material).

Survival analysis revealed that H3.3A K27M-mutant PPK 
tumor bearing mice (n = 15) had significantly reduced sur-
vival compared to PPW (n = 10) (Figure 1C). Additionally, 
immunohistochemistry (IHC) analyses of murine tumors 
showed tumor-specific expression of H3K27M and global 
loss of H3K27me3 expression, a salient feature of H3K27M-
DMG (Figure 1D).19 RNA-sequencing of PPK and PPW 
showed elevated ID1 expression in PPK tumors (Figure 1E). 
Further, western blot analysis confirmed increased ID1 ex-
pression in a PPK tumor-derived cell line (Figure 1F).
ID1 Expression is Influenced by H3 Mutational 
Status and Associated with Lower Overall 
Survival in DMG
In whole transcriptome sequencing from 34 DMG and 18 
normal brain samples (cortex), DMG tissue showed sig-
nificantly higher ID1 expression (Figure 1G). ScRNA-seq 
data from H3K27M-mutant DMGs [Dana-Farber Cancer 
Institute (DFCI) cohort20] confirmed that malignant cells 
display significantly higher ID1 expression compared 
to nonmalignant cells within these tumors (Fig. S1A-B). 
ScRNA-seq data from H3K27M-DMG patients (n  =  4) re-
vealed higher ID1 expression in brainstem H3K27M-DMG 
cells compared to thalamic and cortical tumor cells (Figure 
1H), although the number of thalamic tumors (n = 2) is very 
low. Further analysis of bulk RNA-seq [ICR cohort (Institute 
for Cancer Research), n = 22121], in which both brainstem 
and thalamic DMG tumors showed significantly higher 
ID1 expression than cortical pHGGs (Figure 1I). Further, 
H3K27M-DMG patients with higher ID1 expression (ICR co-
hort) have lower OS22 (Figure 1J).
Analysis of bulk tumor RNA-seq (ICR cohort) revealed that 
ID1 expression is significantly increased in DMGs harboring 
H3K27M (H3.3A or H3C2) compared to H3.3WT and H3.3G34R/V 
(Figure 1K).21 ACVR1-mutant tumors have significantly higher 
ID1 expression compared to WT tumors (Figure 1L), but the ad-
dition of mutated ACVR1 to H3 doesn’t significantly increase 
ID1 expression (Figure 1M). Further, western blot analysis of 
two isogenic cell lines DIPGXIIIP K27M-KO vs DIPGXIIIP and 
BT245 K27M-KO vs K27M shows that ID1 expression de-
creases when H3K27M is knocked out (Figure 1N–O).
Epigenetic State of ID1 Loci in DMG Tumor Cells 
by H3 Mutational Status
As DMGs are driven by epigenetic dysregulation, we 
sought to assess H3K27ac and H3K27me3 marks at 
regulatory regions of the ID1 gene in human DMG tumors. 
ChIP-sequencing on normal pediatric pontine tissue (n = 1), 
H3WT DMG (n = 1), and H3K27M DMG (n = 4) tumor sam-
ples revealed a marked increase in H3K27ac deposition at 
ID1 gene body elements in H3K27M DMG tissue (Figure 
2A). Subsequent ChIP-qPCR analysis confirmed signifi-
cantly elevated H3K27ac at predicted promotor and gene 
body regions of the ID1 locus compared to H3WT/ACVR1WT 
DMG samples (Figure 2B–C) (Supplementary Table 1). 
Changes in H3K27me3 were less notable (Figure 2D). 
Further, qPCR of tumor tissue demonstrated ID1 expres-
sion to be highest in H3K27M tumors (n = 4 sites) regard-
less of ACVR1 status (Figure 2E and Fig. S2A-C). We noted 
differences in ID1 expression (qPCR) between multi-focal 
autopsy samples, leading us to analyze multi-focal (n = 6) 
bulk RNA-sequencing of a single H3K27M/ACVR1-mutant 
DMG patient (UMPED12), which revealed varying levels 
of ID1 expression across different regions of the tumor 
(Figure 2F). Assessment of ID1 expression across all malig-
nant cell types in scRNA-seq performed on four DMG pa-
tients showed that ID1 is most highly expressed in DMG 
cells with an astrocytic differentiation program [“AC-like 
cells” 20], followed by oligodendrocyte precursor cell-like 
(“OPC-like”) cells (Figure 2G and Fig. S3A). We observed 
higher levels of ID1 expression in cycling compared to 
noncycling malignant cells (Fig. S3B).
ID1+ Malignant DMG Cells Share Transcriptional 
Program with OAPC-like Cells in Developing 
Human Brain
We next assessed ID1 expression and deposition of 
H3K27ac at the ID1 gene locus across pre and postnatal 
mouse brain developmental stages. RNA in-situ hybridi-
zation data (Allen Brain Atlas) demonstrated that ID1 RNA 
was higher in the developing prenatal mouse hindbrain 
(including developing pons) compared to forebrain or mid-
brain, and postnatal mouse brain (Figure 3A–B and Fig. 
S4). ChIP-sequencing in E15.5 mouse brains revealed ele-
vated H3K27ac in the hindbrain compared to midbrain and 
forebrain,23 including at ID1 enhancer sites (Fig. S5A-B).
Analysis of developing human24 and mouse25 brain 
scRNA-seq data showed that ID1 expression peaks at ges-
tational week (GW) 12–22 in the human pons (Figure 3C) 
and early postnatal mouse pons (P0; Fig. S6A-D), and is 
most highly expressed in astrocytes. IHC analyses of pre 
and postnatal brains confirmed elevated ID1 in the mu-
rine embryonic brain (E18; Figure 3D) and human GW20.5 
brain (Figure 3E) in subventricular regions lining the 4th 
ventricle.

We next sought to assess whether ID1+ sub-
populations of malignant DMG cells share a tran-
scriptional program with ID1+ developing brain cells. 
Interestingly, AC-like cells from all four DMG tumors 
show the strongest overlap with the transcriptional 
program of the recently defined OAPC cell population 
in the developing human brain (Figure 3F). OAPCs ex-
press both astrocyte (GFAP) and oligodendrocyte 
(OLIG1, OLIG2) marker genes as well as SPARCL1, 
which is involved in regulation of cell adhesion/migra-
tion. We found ID1 to be a marker gene for both AC-like 
DMG cells and OAPCs. Immunofluorescence and IHC of 
human H3K27M-DMG samples revealed colocalization 
of ID1 and SPARCL1 expression in cell sub-populations 
(Figure 3G).
In vitro ID1-knockdown Decreases Invasion and 
Migration of DMG Cells
Single cell RNA-seq analysis of ID1-expressing AC-like 
DMG cells from human tumors and analysis of bulk 
RNA-seq from mouse IUE-PPK tumors revealed elevated 
SPARCL1 expression (Fig. S7A-B), and enrichment of gene 
sets involved in regulation of cell adhesion and migration 
(Fig. S7C). To explore ID1’s role in DMG cell migration and 
invasion, we pursued genetic (shRNA) and pharmaco-
logic knockdown of ID1 in patient-derived H3K27M-mutant 
DMG cells. CBD (the nonpsychoactive compound found 
in Cannabis sativa26–28) has been shown to reduce ID1 ex-
pression in multiple preclinical solid tumor models,9,29 po-
tentially through increased intracellular levels of reactive 
oxygen species (ROS).30 Genetic knockdown (shID1) in 
DIPG007 resulted in significant ID1 reduction (Figure 4A). 
CBD reduced ID1 protein levels in two K27M-DMG cell cul-
tures (Figure 4B) and murine H3.3-PPK cell culture (Fig. 
S8A), but not in two control [NHA (normal human astro-
cytes) and KNS42 (hemispheric HGG)] cell lines without 
K27M mutation (Fig. S8B). ID1 knockdown resulted in 
SPARCL1 reduction in DIPG007 cells (Figure 4C), further 
indicating that SPARCL1 functions downstream of ID1. CBD 
treatment increased ROS levels in DIPG007 cells treated 
with 2.5 or 5.0 μM of CBD (Figure 4D). Additional treatment 
with Vitamin E [α-tocopherol (TOC)], an established ROS 
scavenger,29,30 consistently rescued the downregulation of 
ID1 expression seen with CBD treatment (Figure 4E).
Genetic- (Sh-ID1) and CBD-mediated ID1-inhibition sig-
nificantly reduced invasion of multiple DMG cell lines in-
cluding DIPG007 (Figure 4F and Fig. S9A-B), PBT-29 (Figure 
4G), and JUMP4 (Fig. S11A-B) but CBD did not reduce in-
vasion of control cell line (NHA and KNS42) to the same 
extent (Fig. S10A-B). ID1 knockdown decreased the effi-
cacy of CBD-mediated invasion reduction (Fig. S9C-E). 
Proliferation rates were unchanged by shID1, but CBD did 
impact cell proliferation of multiple human DMG (DIPG007, 
PBT-29, DIPGXIIIP*, and JUMP4) and mouse PPK cells (Fig. 
S8C-E and S11A,C,E). Rescue of ID1 with the addition of 
TOC blunted the CBD-induced invasion reduction (Figure 
4H). ID1-knockdown significantly reduced DIPG007 migra-
tion using a “scratch assay,” (Figure 4I) and CBD treatment 
significantly reduced migration in three DMG cell lines 
(Figure 4J, Fig. S11D,F,G) when compared to control cells 
(NHA and KNS42) (Fig. S10C). Similar to CBD-induced in-
vasion reduction, rescue of ID1 with TOC also blunted the 
CBD-induced migration reduction (Figure 4J). Genetic 
knockdown of ID1 (shID1) in DIPG007 cells decreased 
sensitivity to CBD treatment in a scratch assay (Figure 
4K–L), indicating that CBD, in part, mediates cell migration 
through ID1.
In vivo Genetic Knockdown of ID1 Increase 
Survival of Mice with pHGG in IUE Model
To assess whether ID1 suppression would impede in vivo 
tumor growth in PPK tumor mice, we knocked down ID1 
expression in our both H3.3-PPK and H3.1-PPK-IUE tumor 
model using PiggyBac transposon ID1-shRNA plasmids 
and scrambled short hairpins (“Sh-control”). Both H3.3-
PPK-ShID1 and H3.1-PPK mice exhibited significantly pro-
longed survival and reduced luminescent tumor signals 
when compared to PPK-control (Figure 5A–C and 5G-H 
and Fig. S13C). H3.3-PPK-Sh-ID1 tumors demonstrated re-
ductions in ID1 and Ki67 expression by IHC (Fig. S12A-B). 
In a human patient-derived intracranial xenograft in vivo 
mouse model, orthotopic implantation of DIPG007 cells 
with ID1-knockdown into the brainstem of NSG mice 
also demonstrated reduced tumor growth compared to 
DIPG007-Sh-control cells, as shown by bioluminescent im-
aging (Fig. S12C-D) and demonstrated reductions in ID1 
and Ki67 expression by IHC (Fig. S12E-F). Orthotopic im-
plantation of human DIPGXIIIP* cells showed increased 
survival in ID1 KD tumor bearing mice when compared to 
controls (Fig. S12G).
We then assessed the impact of CBD treatment on in vivo 
tumor growth using our H3.3- and H3.1-PPK-IUE model. 
Both PPK-IUE mice received daily treatment with CBD 
(15 mg/kg) or vehicle control. CBD treatment significantly 
improved median survival compared to vehicle control 
(Figure 5D and G–H). Further Moribund PPK tumors treated 
with CBD showed reductions in ID1 and Ki67 expression by 
IHC (Figure 5E) and more distinct tumor borders, indicating

CBD Dose Reporting in DMG Patients
CBD is a supplemental nonprescribed therapy gaining use 
among patients with pHGG.31 We gathered patient-reported 
CBD alongside tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) dosing from 
families of DMG patients at two institutions (n = 14 total, 
n = 11, DMG with K27M, n = 3, H3WT), including a med-
ical marijuana therapy registry study (NCT03052738) at 
Children’s Hospital of Colorado and retrospective inter-
views with families of patients who underwent research 
autopsy at the University of Michigan. CBD was given 
orally in all but one case (suppository) one to three times 
per day with a wide range of dosing (0.07 mg/kg to 25 mg/
kg/day) (Fig. S14). This CBD dosing data represents feasi-
bility of CBD treatment in DMG, with the clear need for fur-
ther investigation and prospective therapeutic clinical trial.
publications.conclusions:
Overexpression of the Inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1) gene 
has been tied to the pathogenesis of multiple human can-
cers.32–34 A role for ID1 in DMG has been proposed, based 
on its association with activating mutations in ACVR1, 
which increase ID1 expression through the activation of 
the BMP signaling pathway.10,12,13 Our data show that in 
DMG tissue, ID1 expression is increased with H3K27M 
mutation with minimal additional impact from concurrent 
ACVR1 mutation. This raises the possibility that the epige-
netic activation of the ID1 locus may be the primary driver 
of ID1 signaling in human DMG tumors. Additionally, our 
data support that ID1+/SPARCL1+ expressing AC-like DMG 
cells share a migratory expression transcriptional profile 
with a subset of developing brain cells, the recently iden-
tified OAPCs. This may indicate new and exciting develop-
mental origins for this subset of DMG cells. Further, our 
data indicate that ID1 promotes migration and invasion 
in DMG cells, which are disease-defining features of this 
infiltrative tumor.
We propose a model by which ID1 is upregulated through 
multiple mechanisms to “re-activate” prenatal brain devel-
opmental signaling (Figure 6, upper panel). Further, our 
data suggest that CBD inhibits DMG cell proliferation, in-
vasion, and migration, through both ID1-dependent and 
ID1-independent mechanisms, with inhibition of migra-
tion being the most ID1-dependent and inhibition of pro-
liferation being the most ID1-independent (Figure 6, lower 
panel). Our studies implicate an active epigenetic state at 
the ID1 locus shared between H3K27M tumor cells and 
prenatal precursor brain cells. This is consistent with prior 
studies focused on H3K27M mutations that have associated 
changes in H3K27ac/H3K27me3 with differential regulation 
of key DMG-associated genes.35,36 Additionally, we provide 
evidence that postnatal activation of ID1 in tumor cells rep-
licates a prenatal “migratory” transcriptional state seen 
in a recently discovered subset of developing OAPC brain 
cells. These OAPCs (Olig2+ SPARCL1+ glial progenitor cells) 
were identified as astrocyte-like at the molecular and tran-
scriptional levels. In line with this, we found AC-like DMG 
cells to transcriptionally mimic the program of OAPCs, with 
the OAPC-marker SPARCL1 and ID1 colocalizing in a subset 
of H3K27M tumor cells. Interestingly, previous work has 
suggested a role for SPARCL1 in promoting DMG cell inva-
sion into the subventricular zone (SVZ).37 Our data demon-
strate that ID1 is most highly expressed by cycling AC-like 
cells in DMG tumors and SPARCL1 is one of the strongest 
expression markers of these cells.
Our data show that ID1-knockdown has the potential to 
severely impede DMG tumor cell migration and invasion 
in preclinical models. These phenotypes are consistent 
with the inherent invasion into normal brainstem tissue 
that is observed histologically in DMGs, and with the role 
of ID1 in other cancers.8,34 In our experiments involving 
both genetically-engineered and intracranial implantation 
models, H3K27M-mutant tumor cells with ID1 reduction 
show decreased tumor growth and invasion. Our data raise 
important insights into the mechanisms underlying one of 
the most critical and problematic features of DMG tumors.
In the present study, CBD reduced ID1 expression in 
DMG cells at concentrations that are likely clinically achiev-
able in the human brain. CBD is an often-unregulated 
supplemental therapy already being used for palliative 
treatment in pediatric oncology. It is commonly taken 
alongside THC, though the effects of coadministration are 
unknown in DMG patients. Our data show that CBD treat-
ment reduces ID1 expression and DMG cell invasion and 
migration through increasing intracellular levels of ROS. 
Additionally, CBD increases expression of ATF3 (data not 
shown), which could be another possible mechanism by 
which CBD inhibits ID1 expression in DMG cells.38

publications.title: Cannabidiol inhibits RAD51 and sensitizes glioblastoma to temozolomide in multiple orthotopic tumor models
publications.abstract:
Background.  Cannabidiol (CBD), a nonpsychoactive cannabinoid with a low toxicity profile, has been shown to 
produce antitumor activity across cancers in part through selective production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in 
tumor cells. The alkylating agent, temozolomide (TMZ), is standard of care for treatment of glioblastoma (GBM). It 
can trigger increased ROS to induce DNA damage. It has also been reported that downregulating the expression 
of RAD51, an important DNA damage repair protein, leads to sensitization of GBM to TMZ.
Methods. We determined the extent to which CBD enhanced the antitumor activity of TMZ in multiple orthotopic 
models of GBM. In addition, we investigated the potential for CBD to enhance the antitumor activity of TMZ through 
production of ROS and modulation of DNA repair pathways.
Results.  CBD enhanced the activity of TMZ in U87 MG and U251 GBM cell lines and in patient-derived primary 
GBM163 cells leading to stimulation of ROS, activation of the ROS sensor AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), 
and upregulation of the autophagy marker LC3A. CBD produced a sensitization of U87 and GBM163-derived in­
tracranial (i.c.) tumors to TMZ and significantly increased survival of tumor-bearing mice. However, these effects 
were not observed in orthotopic models derived from GBM with intact methylguanine methyltransferase (MGMT) 
expression. We further demonstrate that CBD inhibited RAD51 expression in MGMT-methylated models of GBM, 
providing a potential mechanism for tumor sensitization to TMZ by CBD.
Conclusion. These data support the potential therapeutic benefits of using CBD to enhance the antitumor activity 
of TMZ in GBM patients.
Key Points
•	 CBD produces enhancement of TMZ antitumor activity selectively in MGMT-methylated 
GBM leading to prolong survival. 
•	 CBD inhibited RAD51 expression in MGMT-methylated GBM, providing a potential 
mechanism for tumor sensitization to TMZ by CBD.
In the management of glioblastoma (GBM), surgery with 
postoperative radio- and chemotherapy, primarily with the 
alkylating agent temozolomide (TMZ), are the treatment of 
choice.1 Additional tumor treatment modalities have also been 
FDA approved for the treatment of GBM.2 Despite these ag­
gressive treatments, 90% of the patients die within 2  years.1 
Specifically, patients with an unmethylated O6-methylguanine–
DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter respond poorly 
Cannabidiol inhibits RAD51 and sensitizes glioblastoma 
to temozolomide in multiple orthotopic tumor models
   
 2
Soroceanu et al. Cannabidiol sensitizes glioblastoma to temozolomide
to alkylating agents such as TMZ.3 Thus, there is an urgent 
need for novel therapeutics strategies targeting GBM.
The cannabinoid (CB) Δ 9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) ac­
tivates 2 known CB receptors (CB1 and CB2), which leads 
to the inhibition of cell proliferation and induction of ap­
optosis resulting in the reduction of tumor burden in vivo 
in multiple cancers, including GBM.4–6 These antitumor 
effects of CB1 and CB2 receptor agonists are thought to 
occur primarily through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) 
stress-dependent upregulation of autophagy-mediated 
cell death pathways (a caspase-independent form of pro­
grammed cell death).6–8 However, the clinical utility of THC 
is limited by its psychoactive effects. There are more than 
60 CBs in Cannabis sativa and a majority are not psycho­
active.9 Nonpsychoactive CBs found in reasonable abun­
dance include cannabidiol (CBD), cannabigerol (CBG), and 
cannabichromene (CBC).9 CBD has negligible affinity for 
the cloned CB1 and CB2 receptors and does not directly 
target the classical endoCB system.10–12 We determined 
that in a screen of plant-based cannabiniods, that CBD was 
the most active at inhibiting cell viability/proliferation (vi­
ability) in cancer lines from different origins.13 This effect 
has been shown to exhibit significantly lower potency in 
noncancer cells.14 The initial site CBD interacts with to pro­
duce antitumor activity is unknown. Multiple target sites 
have been implicated,15 but the most unifying downstream 
mechanism in culture is the initial CBD-dependent selec­
tive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in tumor 
cells.16
This led us to hypothesize that nonpsychoactive CBs 
could be as effective as psychoactive CBs at inhibiting 
cancer progression and could reduce or replace the 
amount of psychoactive CBs used in the treatment of 
cancer. In support of this hypothesis, we previously re­
ported that CBD can reduce the concentration of THC 
needed to inhibit GBM cell growth and induce apoptosis 
in culture.17 This result was confirmed by additional investi­
gations in vivo18 in subcutaneous xenograft tumor models, 
while our group has also demonstrated that CBD alone can 
inhibit human GBM progression in an intracranial xeno­
graft mouse model.19
As a result of the growing preclinical body of evidence 
of direct antitumor activity produced by THC and CBD, 
multiple clinical trials have evaluated the activity of CBs 
in GBM. In a pilot study, intracranially administered THC 
was shown to be safe, in addition to inhibiting markers of 
tumor cell proliferation.20 Sativex, a plant-based extract 
containing a 1:1 ratio of THC:CBD, was also shown to pro­
long survival for GBM patients in a Phase IIb clinical trial, 
but the detailed results of the trial have not been publish.21 
The direct antitumor activity produced by CBD has also 
recently been evaluated in clinical case studies across can­
cers, including GBM. Clinical responses were observed in a 
significant subset of patients supporting the need for future 
controlled clinical trials.22,23 Taken together, these findings 
underscore the importance of understanding mechanims 
of CB antitumor activity, which may further improve the ac­
tivity of the CBs and potentially lead to the development of 
more active second-generation compounds.
In this study, we investigated the antitumor activity 
of CBs alone and in combination with TMZ for targeting 
GBM progression in intracranial models using GBM cell 
lines and primary patient-derived GBM. In comparison 
to standard GBM cell lines, primary patient-derived GBM

Results
CBD Enhances the Activity of TMZ in U87and 
U251 GBM Cells
We determined whether CBD could enhance the activity 
of the first-line agent TMZ by evaluating the effects of the 
drugs alone or in combination (Figure 1A and B). U87 and 
U251 cells were treated for 3 days with a range of concen­
trations of either CBD, TMZ, or CBD + TMZ and the ability 
of the drugs to inhibit cell viability was assessed using the 
MTT assay. Using the calculated IC50 values, various dose 
ratios of CBD and TMZ were combined in both U87 and 
U251 cells, and viability was evaluated and a CI throughout 
the dose ratios was calculated (Figure 1C). A CI value of <1, 
1, and >1 indicates synergism, additivity, and antagonism, 
respectively.30 The combination of CBD and TMZ led prima­
rily to additive inhibition of cell viability across multiple 
dose ratios in U87 and U251 cells.
CBD-Dependent Stimulation of ROS Leads to 
Inhibition of GBM Cell Viability
CBD produces a sustained upregulation of ROS in a 
concentration-dependent manner in U251 GBM cells 
leading to inhibition of cell viability (Figure 1D). This effect

blocked by TOC (Figure 1F). The ability of CBs to sensitize 
GBM to TMZ in orthotopic models has not been evaluate; 
therefore, we next studied the effects of CBs to sensitize 
human GBM to TMZ in vivo.
CBs Sensitize Human U87-Derived Intracranial 
Tumors to TMZ
We evaluated the ability of CBD alone or CBD + THC in a 
1:1 ratio (CBD/THC) in combination with TMZ to inhibit 
tumor growth and extend survival in an intracranial (i.c.) 
model of GBM utilizing human U87 cells. In vivo imaging 
of luciferase-labeled U87 cells evaluated reduction in ra­
diance (indirect measure of tumor size) in each treatment 
group (Figure 2A and B). CBD or CBD/THC did not inhibit 
GBM progression; however, these CBs produced a sen­
sitization of U87-derived tumors to TMZ, leading to more 
effective inhibition of tumor progression and prolonged 
survival (Figure 2C). The mean survival for vehicle, CBD, 
CBD/THC, TMZ, CBD + TMZ, and CBD/THC + TMZ was 39, 43, 
40, 46, 53, and 53 days, respectively (Figure 2C). Treatment 
with CBD + TMZ (P < .043) or CBD/THC + TMZ (P < .030) pro­
duced a significant improvement in survival in comparison 
to treatment with TMZ alone. Treatment with CBD + TMZ 
also produced full regression in 2 of the 11 tumors.
To determine whether the effect of CBD in vivo was 
dose dependent, we treated mice bearing U87-derived i.c. 
tumors with 3.75 and 7.5 mg/kg of CBD alone or in com­
bination with TMZ (Figure 2D and E). We observed full re­
gression of a tumor in 1 of 11 mice in the CBD treatment 
group but overall there was no significant increase in sur­
vival in this group compared to control. We also observed 
full regression of tumor growth in 2 of 11 mice in the TMZ-
treated group. In contrast to 15 mg/kg of CBD (Figure 2C), 
lower doses of CBs did not enhance the antitumor activity 
of TMZ in an orthotopic mouse model of human GBM. 
These data demonstrate that the ability of CBD to en­
hance the antitumor activity of TMZ is dose dependent. PK 
parameters for CBD in plasma (Supplementary Table 1 and

(Figure 4C), and treatment with TMZ alone prolonged 
survival (P < .02). CBD treatment increased animal sur­

FOXM1 inhibition sensitizes resistant brain cancer cells to 
the first-line DNA damage agent TMZ by downregulating 
the expression of RAD51 gene, which encodes an important 
DNA damage repair protein.37 Our recently published work 
demonstrated that across multiple cancers CBD regulated 
a consistent set of transcription factors controlling tumor 
progression, including FOXM1.38 We therefore investigated 
whether CBD regulates the FOXM1-RAD51 pathway in this 
study. In TMZ-sensitive lines U87 and GBM163X (Figure 5A 
and B), CBD effectively inhibited RAD51 expression when 
cells were treated with CBD alone or in combination with 
TMZ. In contrast, CBD was ineffective at downregulating 
RAD51 upon cotreatment with TMZ in TMZ-resistant cells 
(Figure 5C and D). The inhibitory effects of CBD on FOXM1 
expression were only observed in the CBD alone treatment 
group in GBM163X, suggesting this target was not consist­
ently modulated in either TMZ-sensitive or resistant GBM.
In the presence of the ROS scavenger TOC, CBD was 
not effective at downregulating RAD51 in GBM163X 
demonstrating dependence on production of ROS 
(Supplementary Figure 3A and B). RAD51 levels were 
also modulated by the combination of CBD and TMZ in 
vivo, following treatment of mice bearing GBM163X in­
tracranial tumors with 15  mg/kg CBD and 2  mg/kg TMZ 
(Supplementary Figure 4).
